title: Gossip
hookLine: Pope Francis warned again and again against gossip
tomorrow: Sofia has to give a toast saturday. what does she say?

cards: A screenshot lands with three words on top: don't tell anyone. By lunch it's in four more chats. Nobody feels like they started anything; each person only passed it along.
So why does a rumor need you to keep it alive? Because it can't travel on its own. Every move it makes, somebody carries it.
And Pope Francis, among others, kept telling people to stop carrying.

teach.b: Proverbs gives the picture, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "When the wood faileth, the fire shall go out: and when the talebearer is taken away, contentions shall cease." A rumor is a fire.
It can't feed itself; it needs the next stick.

teach.h: A SMALL FIRE, A GREAT WOOD.
teach.b: James says the tongue works the same way: "Behold how small a fire kindleth a great wood."
Gossip rarely feels like setting anything on fire. It feels like news, like being in the loop. Sometimes it even arrives dressed as concern: did you hear, pray for her.
Pope Francis was blunt about it, once calling gossip a plague. The Catechism names two sins close by. Calumny is telling lies that hurt someone's name.
Detraction is telling someone's real faults, without a good reason, to people who didn't know. Notice that detraction can be true.
Calumny is easy to spot; detraction hides behind the word true. So the question isn't only whether it's accurate, but whether it needed saying.

Before passing anything on, one question does most of the work: does the person hearing it need it? The fire goes out when one person stops adding wood, and that person can be whoever is holding the phone.

how: Catholics examine their speech against the eighth commandment, which the Catechism says forbids calumny and detraction, and confess gossip in the sacrament of Penance.

o: telling a lie under oath in court
a private chat between close friends
talk about someone that didn't need saying

games.q: the fire and the wood — tap the pairs.
p: what a rumor needs to keep burning

s: if it's true, it isn't gossip
the Catechism's detraction is telling someone's real faults without a good reason.
Proverbs pictures a rumor as a fire that goes out without wood
when the talebearer is taken away, contentions shall cease.
passing a rumor along is harmless if you didn't start it
the fire burns on whatever wood each person adds.

games.q: in the family group chat, an aunt posts that a cousin 'is having money problems, pray for her!!' and asks what everyone knows. what keeps the fire small?
o: pray if you pray, and add no details or forwards.
share what you've heard too, so the family has it all.
reply that she's surely exaggerating, to calm things down.
games.why: even a prayer request can carry wood. the talebearer taken away is the person who lets it stop with them.

practice: Close your eyes and let one piece of news about someone come to mind, something you heard and could pass on. Notice the small itch to tell it.
Then set it down, like a stick you've decided not to throw on the fire, and stay with the quiet that's left. If it comes up later, change the subject: the simplest way to take the talebearer away.

wordCard.voice: Gossip. Talk about someone who isn't there that didn't need saying, true or not, carried from one chat to the next.

orig.note: Latin: the Church's word for telling someone's true faults without need.

carryVoice: The line to keep: not repeated, since a fire with no more wood goes out. See you next week.
